title: Oral & Written Traditions
description: From bards and scribes to scrolls and codices — pre-print information ecosystems

concepts.title: Before Writing: Oral Cultures
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of human history, all information moved by mouth. Stories, laws, genealogies, agricultural knowledge, and religious lore lived only in the memory of speakers. To survive across generations, this knowledge had to be encoded for memory: rhythm, meter, formulaic phrases, parallelism, and song.

Homer's Iliad and Odyssey were composed and transmitted orally for centuries before they were written down (probably around the 8th century BCE). The American classicist Milman Parry showed in the 1930s that Homeric verse is built from a vast inventory of stock phrases — "swift-footed Achilles," "wine-dark sea" — that allowed poets to compose extempore in performance. Similar systems supported the West African jeli (griot) tradition and Vedic chant in India.

Oral cultures are not "primitive": they sustain enormous quantities of precise knowledge. But the medium shapes the message. Information that cannot be sung or storyed tends not to survive, and there is no stable text to argue with — only the latest performance.

concepts.title: The Invention of Writing
concepts.contentHtml:
Writing was invented independently at least three or four times: in Sumer around 3200 BCE (cuneiform on clay), in Egypt around the same time (hieroglyphs), in China by 1200 BCE (oracle-bone script), and in Mesoamerica with the Olmec and Maya. The earliest tablets are not poems or prayers — they are accounts: receipts for grain, beer, and labor. Writing began as bookkeeping for centralized states.

Each script reflected its writing surface. Cuneiform's wedge-shaped marks were efficient impressions for a stylus in wet clay. Egyptian hieroglyphs flourished on papyrus. Chinese characters, originally incised on bone, hardened into a logographic system that has survived for over three millennia.

The decisive simplification was the alphabet. Around 1800 BCE, Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt adapted hieroglyphs into a small set of consonant signs. The Phoenicians refined this into a 22-letter system; the Greeks added vowels; the Romans gave us the Latin alphabet. With ~26 reusable symbols, literacy became achievable for non-specialists — a precondition for everything that followed.

concepts.title: Scrolls, Codices, and the Manuscript Order
concepts.contentHtml:
For a thousand years the dominant book form was the scroll — papyrus or parchment unrolled from one rod to another. Scrolls suit continuous reading but resist random access; you cannot quickly flip to chapter 12. The codex — bound pages stitched at one edge, the form modern books still take — emerged in the early Roman Empire and was adopted by early Christians, partly because it let readers jump between Old and New Testament passages.

Books were astonishingly expensive. A single Bible could require the skins of 200 sheep and a year of a scribe's labor. Production was concentrated in monastic scriptoria in Europe, in caliphal libraries like the House of Wisdom in 9th-century Baghdad, and in Buddhist monasteries across East Asia, where wood-block printing was already in use by the 8th century.

This was an information order shaped by scarcity. Most knowledge passed orally, in apprenticeships and sermons; the written record was thin, controlled by clerical and state elites, and copied with the small errors and editorial choices that copying entails. Authority lay with institutions that controlled the manuscripts — the church, the court, the madrasa.

title: The Printing Revolution
description: Gutenberg, print capitalism, the Reformation, the rise of the public

concepts.title: Gutenberg and Movable Type
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1450, in Mainz, the goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg combined three existing technologies into something new: a screw press adapted from winemaking, an oil-based ink that adhered to metal, and — the critical piece — movable type cast from a hand mould that could produce thousands of identical, reusable letters. His 42-Line Bible (c. 1455) was the first major Western book printed this way.

Movable type had earlier precedents in East Asia. The Korean Jikji, printed with metal type in 1377, predates Gutenberg by nearly a century. But the alphabetic European context multiplied the technique's leverage: a Latin font needed only a few hundred sorts, while a Chinese font needed thousands.

The economic effect was startling. Producing a book that had cost a year of scribal labor now cost a few days of press work. A single press could output several hundred copies of a text in the time it took a scribe to copy one. Within fifty years there were printing presses in over 250 European cities; an estimated 8 million books had been printed by 1500 — more than European scribes had produced in the entire previous millennium.

concepts.title: Print Capitalism and the Reformation
concepts.contentHtml:
Print did not just speed up book production; it created a new commercial industry. Printers were entrepreneurs who chose what to publish based on what would sell. The historian Benedict Anderson later coined the term print capitalism to describe how, by standardizing vernacular languages (English, French, German) into stable printed forms, the press helped create the "imagined communities" we call modern nations.

The most consequential early test came in 1517, when an obscure Augustinian friar named Martin Luther nailed (or possibly mailed) ninety-five theses against the sale of indulgences to a church door in Wittenberg. Without print, this would have been a local academic dispute. With print, Luther's pamphlets — short, vernacular, often illustrated with anti-papal woodcuts — sold an estimated 300,000 copies in three years. The Reformation was the first mass media event.

The Catholic Church and Catholic monarchies responded with the Index Librorum Prohibitorum (1559), the first formal list of banned books, and with state licensing of printers. The pattern of cheap print followed by attempted state control would repeat with every new medium for the next five centuries.

concepts.title: The Birth of the Newspaper
concepts.contentHtml:
The first recognizable newspapers emerged in early-17th-century Europe. Relation aller Fürnemmen und gedenckwürdigen Historien, printed in Strasbourg from 1605, is generally credited as the first weekly. The Daily Courant began in London in 1702 — the first English-language daily.

These early papers reported on foreign wars, court news, and shipping movements for an audience of merchants and officials. They depended on the postal system, which had been built up across Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries to serve the same commercial and diplomatic class. The newspaper and the modern post office grew up together.

By the 18th century, papers and pamphlets had become central to political life. In Britain, coffeehouses circulated papers for shared reading and debate; the philosopher Jürgen Habermas later argued these venues constituted a new bourgeois public sphere in which private people came together as a public to scrutinize the state. In the American colonies, papers like the Pennsylvania Gazette carried the arguments — and accusations — that prepared revolution. Print had turned readers into a political constituency.

title: The Penny Press & Mass Newspapers
description: 19th-century cheap newspapers, telegraph wires, and the birth of mass media

concepts.title: The Penny Press: News as a Commodity
concepts.contentHtml:
For their first two centuries, newspapers were a tool of merchants and political elites. A subscription to a New York paper in the 1820s cost 6 cents an issue at a time when a skilled worker earned around 85 cents a day — well beyond ordinary readers.

That changed in 1833 when the printer Benjamin Day launched the New York Sun, sold on the street by newsboys for one penny. Day's insight was to fund the paper not by subscriptions from a small loyal audience but by advertising sold against a mass audience. To reach that audience, the Sun covered crime, scandal, human-interest stories, and famously the "Great Moon Hoax" of 1835 — fabricated reports of bat-people on the lunar surface that doubled circulation.

The penny press was made possible by new technology: the steam-driven cylinder press, capable of thousands of impressions per hour, and cheap pulp paper. By 1840 the genre had spread to Boston and Philadelphia; by 1860 the New York Herald had a circulation of 77,000, the largest in the world. The modern newspaper as a mass-market commercial product was born.

concepts.title: Wires, Speed, and the News Agency
concepts.contentHtml:
News had always travelled at the speed of horses or sailing ships. Samuel Morse's working telegraph (first commercial line, Baltimore–Washington, 1844) collapsed that delay. By 1858, a transatlantic cable linked New York to London; by the 1870s a global wire network connected the major capitals.

Wire transmission was expensive per word, which gave news a new style: short, factual, front-loaded — the inverted pyramid still taught in journalism schools. It also created a new business — the news agency. Charles-Louis Havas founded what became Agence France-Presse in Paris in 1835; his ex-employees Paul Reuter and Bernhard Wolff founded Reuters (London, 1851) and the Wolff agency (Berlin). In the US, six New York papers pooled telegraph costs to form what became the Associated Press (1846).

Agencies sold the same wire copy to dozens of papers, which encouraged a tone of impersonal, "just the facts" reporting that could pass without offending any single client's politics. Objectivity as a journalistic norm has many fathers, but the wire bill is one of them.

concepts.title: Yellow Journalism and the Mass Audience
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1890s the press was big business and circulation wars were ferocious. In New York, Joseph Pulitzer's World and William Randolph Hearst's Journal battled for readers with banner headlines, color comics, sensational crime coverage, and crusading exposés — the style critics christened "yellow journalism" after the Yellow Kid comic both papers ran.

Pulitzer and Hearst's coverage of the explosion of the USS Maine in Havana harbor in 1898 — "Remember the Maine, To Hell with Spain" — is widely credited with helping push the United States into the Spanish-American War, the textbook case of a press inflaming public opinion. Whether the war would have happened anyway is debated; that the press now had the reach and intensity to matter, no one disputes.

The same era produced reform: the muckrakers. Journalists like Ida Tarbell (Standard Oil), Lincoln Steffens (urban political machines), and Upton Sinclair (the meatpacking industry, in The Jungle, 1906) used long-form investigation to drive antitrust action and the Pure Food and Drug Act. By 1900, the press was simultaneously a commercial mass medium, a political weapon, and an emerging instrument of democratic accountability — three roles whose tensions still define journalism.

title: Radio & Cinema
description: Voice and image at scale — Hollywood, the BBC, and wartime broadcasting

concepts.title: Radio: From Wireless Telegraphy to Broadcasting
concepts.contentHtml:
Radio began not as a broadcast medium but as a one-to-one alternative to the telegraph wire. Guglielmo Marconi's 1901 transatlantic transmission carried Morse code, not voice. The shift to broadcasting — one transmitter, many receivers — was a 1920s innovation, and it fundamentally changed what radio was for.

The first commercially licensed broadcaster, KDKA in Pittsburgh, went on the air in November 1920 carrying the Harding–Cox election results. Within a few years there were hundreds of stations in the United States. Two regulatory models emerged. The American system, codified by the Radio Act of 1927 and the Communications Act of 1934, allocated the spectrum to private commercial stations funded by advertising and lightly supervised by the FCC. The British system, embodied in the BBC (chartered 1927 under John Reith's mission to "inform, educate, and entertain"), was a single public-service broadcaster funded by a household licence fee.

Most other countries chose variants of one model or the other. The split — commercial vs public-service broadcasting — would shape television, and is still the central institutional question for media policy a century later.

concepts.title: Cinema and the Studio System
concepts.contentHtml:
The first paid film screening was the Lumière brothers' Cinématographe show in Paris in December 1895 — ten short actualities including a train arriving at La Ciotat station that supposedly sent audiences ducking for cover. Within a decade, cinema had spread worldwide, and within two it had moved from fairground attraction to industrial art form.

By the 1920s, Hollywood dominated. Five vertically integrated studios — MGM, Paramount, Warner Bros., RKO, and 20th Century Fox — owned production lots, distribution networks, and the theaters where their films played. They produced under the studio system: stars on multi-year contracts, in-house writers and directors, films assembled like cars. The transition to sound after The Jazz Singer (1927) cemented Hollywood's lead by raising the capital required to compete.

Cinema reached audiences television would not match for decades: in 1946 the average American went to the movies once a week. The studios' grip eased only after the Paramount antitrust decree of 1948 forced them to divest their theaters, and after television began siphoning audiences away in the 1950s.

concepts.title: Wartime Broadcasting and Propaganda
concepts.contentHtml:
Radio and cinema came of age alongside total war, and governments quickly saw their potential. In Britain, Edward R. Murrow's live CBS broadcasts from London during the Blitz ("This is London") — bombs audible in the background — drew American audiences emotionally into a war their country had not yet entered. In Germany, Joseph Goebbels's Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda subsidized cheap Volksempfänger ("people's receivers") so that nearly every household could tune in to Nazi broadcasts; Leni Riefenstahl's films Triumph of the Will (1935) and Olympia (1938) translated the same message to the screen.

Allied governments were not innocent. The US Office of War Information and Britain's Ministry of Information shaped news coverage, censored film, and produced propaganda explicitly. Frank Capra's Why We Fight series was commissioned by the US Army. The technologies were neutral; the institutional uses were not.

The legacies are dual. After 1945, broadcasting in democracies pivoted toward an ideal of editorial independence — the BBC's wartime credibility was its postwar foundation. But the war demonstrated that sound and image at scale could mobilize whole populations, a lesson that propagandists, advertisers, and election campaigns have not forgotten.

title: The Television Era
description: Three-network America, public broadcasters, and the living-room nation

concepts.title: Television Becomes Mass Culture
concepts.contentHtml:
Television was demonstrated in the 1920s and 1930s but only became a mass medium after 1945, when the wartime electronics industry retooled for consumer goods. In 1950, around 9% of US households owned a television; by 1960 it was 87%. Britain and Western Europe reached saturation a few years later.

In the United States, three commercial networks — NBC, CBS, and ABC — dominated. With only a handful of channels available on the VHF dial, prime-time audiences were enormous: the I Love Lucy finale in 1953 reached an estimated 71% of American TV households; the 1969 Apollo 11 moon landing was watched by an estimated 600 million people worldwide. Television was the medium of the mass national audience in a way print and radio never quite were.

It was also a powerfully commercial medium. The 30-second spot, the prime-time schedule built around advertiser preferences, and the practice of measuring audiences by Nielsen ratings turned attention into a tradable commodity. The same business logic — sell audiences to advertisers — would migrate to digital platforms half a century later.

concepts.title: Public-Service Broadcasting and Cable
concepts.contentHtml:
Outside the United States, the dominant model was a strong public-service broadcaster alongside (or instead of) commercial channels. The BBC in Britain, NHK in Japan, ARD/ZDF in Germany, and the CBC in Canada were funded mostly by household licence fees, charged with serving citizens rather than just consumers, and granted varying degrees of editorial independence. Public-service broadcasting set the news-quality benchmark even where it was a minority of the schedule.

The American near-equivalent, PBS, was created by the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967 — late, underfunded compared to its European peers, but the source of Sesame Street, Frontline, and the lineage of serious public television.

From the late 1970s, cable television dismantled the three-network world. CNN (1980) launched 24-hour news; MTV (1981) gave a generation its visual vernacular; HBO and Showtime introduced subscription-funded prestige drama. Audiences fragmented across hundreds of channels, prime-time ratings collapsed from their 1950s peaks, and the era of every American watching the same evening news ended for good.

concepts.title: Television Politics: From the Living Room to Live News
concepts.contentHtml:
Television transformed political life. The Kennedy–Nixon debate of September 26, 1960 — the first televised US presidential debate — was famously rated a Kennedy win on TV and a Nixon win on radio: appearance and demeanour now mattered as never before. Campaigns rebuilt themselves around the 30-second ad and the photo opportunity.

Live coverage gave wars a new visibility. The Vietnam War was the first "living-room war"; nightly footage of body bags and burning villages corroded public support in a way print never had. After the 1968 Tet Offensive, when CBS anchor Walter Cronkite returned to the studio and called the war "mired in stalemate," President Johnson reportedly told an aide, "If I've lost Cronkite, I've lost middle America."

Television also gave authoritarian and democratic governments new instruments. The Soviet and Chinese systems used a small number of state channels for unified messaging. Western democracies developed elaborate regulatory regimes — equal-time rules, must-carry, and limits on cross-ownership — to manage a medium too powerful to leave entirely to the market or the state. By the time the internet arrived, television had set the template: news as image, politics as performance, and audience attention as the resource everyone competed for.

title: The Internet & Digital Age
description: Web 1.0 to social platforms — disintermediation, fragmentation, and feeds

concepts.title: From ARPANET to the Web
concepts.contentHtml:
The internet's deep roots are military and academic. ARPANET, funded by the US Department of Defense, exchanged its first packets between UCLA and Stanford in 1969. The technical breakthrough was packet switching (independently invented by Paul Baran and Donald Davies in the 1960s): break a message into pieces, route each separately across a redundant mesh, reassemble at the destination. The result was a network with no single point of failure.

Through the 1970s and 1980s, the protocols that bind today's internet — TCP/IP (Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn, 1974), email, FTP, DNS — were standardized and adopted worldwide. The system was open and academic; commercial use was effectively banned until the early 1990s.

The shift to mass medium came in 1989–1991, when Tim Berners-Lee at CERN built the World Wide Web: HTML, HTTP, and the first browser. The 1993 release of the graphical Mosaic browser brought the web to ordinary users. Within five years, dot-com mania, e-commerce, and online news were transforming every adjacent industry — and the open-academic ethos of the early internet was colliding with the commercial logic of the mass media it was about to disrupt.

concepts.title: Web 2.0 and the Platform Era
concepts.contentHtml:
The first wave of the web ("Web 1.0") was mostly read-only: news organisations and companies published pages, users consumed them. From around 2004, what publisher Tim O'Reilly dubbed "Web 2.0" reversed the relationship. The new platforms — Wikipedia (2001), Facebook (2004), YouTube (2005), Twitter (2006), Reddit, blogs — were built on user-generated content, social graphs, and feedback loops.

The economic shift was more important than the technical one. Most platforms were free at the point of use and funded by targeted advertising: the platform tracked behaviour, sold the resulting attention to advertisers, and reinvested the revenue in growth. The smartphone (iPhone 2007, Android shortly after) put a connected camera and feed in nearly every pocket. By the late 2010s, a handful of US firms — Google, Meta, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft — and a few Chinese counterparts (Tencent, Alibaba, Bytedance) intermediated most of the world's online communication.

The disintermediation cut both ways. Citizen journalism, independent creators, and grassroots organising flourished as never before. So did harassment, misinformation, and political manipulation. The platforms that promised to give everyone a voice ended up sitting on top of a more concentrated information stack than the broadcasters they replaced.

concepts.title: Algorithmic Feeds and the AI Turn
concepts.contentHtml:
The decisive change of the 2010s was the move from chronological to algorithmic feeds. Facebook's News Feed (2006), then ranked by the EdgeRank algorithm and its successors; Twitter's "For You" tab; YouTube's recommendation engine; and TikTok's full-screen For You Page (launched in 2018, the most aggressive recommender to date) all replaced "show me the latest from the people I follow" with "show me what the system predicts will keep me watching."

The shift made platforms wildly more engaging — and more politically consequential. Studies from MIT and elsewhere have found that false news travels faster and farther than true news on these systems, in part because outrage and novelty score well on engagement metrics. Foreign influence operations (notably Russia's Internet Research Agency in 2014–2016), domestic disinformation, and conspiracy movements all proved able to exploit the recommendation surface.

The next disruption is already arriving. Generative AI can produce text, images, audio, and video at near-zero marginal cost. Synthetic news articles, voice clones, and deepfaked video raise the question of whether the internet's information stack — already strained — can support the volume of plausible-but-fake content that AI now makes cheap. Whether the answer is technical (provenance, watermarking), regulatory (DSA-style platform liability), or behavioural (relearned scepticism), the short history of the digital age suggests the institutional adjustment will lag the technology by years.
